lessons.title: Creating a Farm Budget and Cash Flow
lessons.body: A budget is a plan for your money. A cash flow shows when money comes in and goes out. Start by listing all your costs for one season. For 1 hectare of tomatoes, you might spend: seeds (2,000 KES), fertiliser (15,000 KES), pesticides (8,000 KES), labour (30,000 KES), and drip irrigation (25,000 KES). Total costs: 80,000 KES. Now estimate your income. If you harvest 20,000 kg and sell at 20 KES per kg, you get 400,000 KES. Your profit before tax is 320,000 KES. But you need to know when you spend and when you earn. Seeds and fertiliser are bought at planting. Labour is weekly. Income comes at harvest. So your cash flow might show a negative balance early on. You need savings or a small loan to cover the first 2 months. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Excel or Google Sheets. Write each month as a column: Month 1, Month 2, etc. List expenses and income under each. At the bottom, calculate your running balance. If it goes negative, you need to adjust: delay a purchase, borrow from a SACCO, or plant a quick crop like spinach to bring early cash. In Africa, many farmers fail because they run out of cash before harvest. A cash flow plan prevents that. Update your budget every month with real numbers. Compare planned vs actual. If you spent 10,000 KES more on labour, find out why. Maybe you hired extra help for weeding. Next season, budget higher. This simple habit turns farming from gambling into a business.

lessons.title: Tracking Expenses and Income
lessons.body: You cannot manage what you do not measure. Every time you spend or earn, write it down. Use a small notebook and a pen. Keep it in your pocket. At the end of each day, record: date, item, amount, and category. Categories: seeds, fertiliser, pesticides, labour, transport, tools, rent, and miscellaneous. For income: date, crop, quantity, unit price, total, and buyer. For example: 15/03/2025, tomatoes, 50 kg, 25 KES/kg, 1,250 KES, Mama Ngina market. If you sell to a trader who pays later, write 'credit' and the expected payment date. At the end of the month, add up all expenses and income. Use a calculator or a phone app like 'Farm Records' or 'AgriTracker'. If you have a smartphone, Google Sheets is free. Create columns: Date, Description, Category, Income, Expense, Balance. At the bottom, sum each column. This shows your profit or loss for the month. Also track your inventory: seeds left, fertiliser bags, harvested produce. This helps you know when to reorder. Many farmers mix personal and farm money. Open a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for the farm. Deposit all sales there. Pay farm expenses from it. This makes tracking easy. At the end of the season, you will know exactly how much you spent and earned. You can then calculate your profit per crop. Without records, you guess. With records, you decide. Start today. Even a simple notebook is enough. Consistency matters more than fancy tools.

lessons.title: Calculating Cost of Production per Crop
lessons.body: Cost of production (COP) is the total cost to produce one unit of crop, like 1 kg of tomatoes. It tells you if you are making a profit. To calculate COP, add all direct and indirect costs for that crop. Direct costs: seeds, fertiliser, pesticides, labour for planting, weeding, harvesting, and packaging. Indirect costs: a share of rent, water, electricity, and depreciation of tools. For 1 hectare of tomatoes, suppose direct costs are 70,000 KES and indirect costs are 10,000 KES. Total cost = 80,000 KES. If you harvest 20,000 kg, your COP per kg = 80,000 / 20,000 = 4 KES per kg. If you sell at 20 KES per kg, your profit per kg is 16 KES. But if you sell at 3 KES per kg, you make a loss. Knowing COP helps you set a minimum selling price. Never sell below COP. For mixed crops, calculate COP per crop separately. For example, you grow tomatoes and kale. Track costs for each. Use a simple table: Crop, Total Cost, Yield (kg), COP per kg. Update it each season. If COP is too high, find ways to reduce: buy inputs in bulk, use compost instead of fertiliser, reduce labour by using mulching. If COP is low, you can undercut competitors. In Africa, many farmers don't know their COP. They sell at whatever price the trader offers. That is risky. With COP, you can negotiate. You can also compare crops: maybe kale has lower COP and higher profit per hectare. Then you plant more kale. This is smart farming. Start calculating COP for your main crop this season.

lessons.title: Break-Even Analysis for the Hectare
lessons.body: Break-even analysis tells you how much you need to sell to cover all your costs. At break-even, profit is zero. Below that, you lose money. Above that, you profit. To calculate break-even, you need fixed costs, variable costs, and selling price. Fixed costs: rent, insurance, depreciation, and salaries. Variable costs: seeds, fertiliser, labour, and packaging. For 1 hectare of tomatoes: fixed costs = 20,000 KES (rent, tools, insurance). Variable cost per kg = 3 KES (seeds, fertiliser, labour, etc.). Selling price per kg = 20 KES. Contribution margin per kg = selling price - variable cost = 20 - 3 = 17 KES. Break-even quantity = fixed costs / contribution margin = 20,000 / 17 = 1,176 kg. So you need to sell at least 1,176 kg to cover all costs. If you expect to harvest 20,000 kg, you are well above break-even. Break-even revenue = break-even quantity x selling price = 1,176 x 20 = 23,529 KES. You can also calculate break-even in terms of yield per hectare. If your yield is below break-even, you lose money. Use this to set targets. If break-even is 1,176 kg and your average yield is 1,000 kg, you need to improve yield or reduce costs. Maybe use better seeds or more fertiliser. Or increase price by selling directly to consumers. Break-even analysis is a simple tool. Do it before planting. Write it in your notebook. Recalculate if costs or prices change. In Africa, where prices fluctuate, break-even helps you decide whether to plant at all. If you cannot break even, plant something else.

lessons.title: Taxes and Insurance for Small Farms
lessons.body: In many African countries, small farms are exempt from taxes if income is below a threshold. For example, in Kenya, agricultural income below 1 million KES per year is not taxed. But you may still pay land rates, market fees, and VAT on inputs. Check with your local tax office. Keep records of all sales and expenses. If you sell to a cooperative or a large buyer, they may deduct withholding tax. You can claim it back if you file returns. Even if you are exempt, it is good to keep records. You may need them for loans or grants. Insurance is often overlooked. Crop insurance protects you against drought, floods, pests, and diseases. In Kenya, the Agriculture Insurance Subsidy Programme (AISP) offers subsidised premiums for maize, wheat, and potatoes. For vegetables, private insurers like Jubilee and APA offer cover. Premiums are usually 5-10% of expected revenue. For 1 hectare of tomatoes with expected revenue of 400,000 KES, premium might be 20,000-40,000 KES. That is a lot, but if disaster strikes, you get compensated. Livestock insurance is also available. If you cannot afford insurance, join a farmer group that pools risk. Some SACCOs offer emergency loans after disasters. Also, consider health insurance for your family. Illness can wipe out farm profits. NHIF in Kenya or similar schemes in other countries cost as little as 500 KES per month. Do not ignore taxes and insurance. They are part of running a business. Talk to other farmers, extension officers, and insurance agents. Understand your obligations and options.

lessons.title: Using Farm Management Software
lessons.body: Farm management software helps you track expenses, income, inventory, and labour. It saves time and reduces errors. Many are free or low-cost. For beginners, start with a simple spreadsheet like Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel. Create tabs for Expenses, Income, Inventory, and Labour. Use formulas to calculate totals and profits. If you have a smartphone, try apps like 'Farmbrite', 'Agrivi', or 'FarmLogs'. These allow you to record activities in the field. For example, you can log fertiliser application with date, amount, and cost. The app calculates cost per hectare. Some apps have offline mode, useful where internet is poor. In Africa, 'Farmerline' and 'Esoko' provide SMS-based services. You can send a text to record a sale and get a summary. 'mFarm' in Kenya helps you track sales and expenses via USSD. Choose a tool that fits your budget and tech comfort. Start simple: a notebook and calculator. Then move to a spreadsheet. Then try an app. The goal is to have accurate data. Use it to make decisions: which crop is most profitable? When to hire labour? How much to plant? Software also helps with record keeping for taxes and loans. Banks like data. If you show clean records, you are more likely to get a loan. Train yourself: watch YouTube tutorials, ask a friend, or take a short course. Many agricultural extension officers can help. Do not be afraid of technology. Start small. Even recording one expense per day is a step forward. Over a season, you will have a clear picture of your farm business.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a farm budget?
options: A) To plan and control farm finances
C) To replace a cash flow statement
D) To apply for a loan
quiz.explanation: A budget is a financial plan that helps you allocate resources and monitor spending.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost for a 1-hectare vegetable farm?
quiz.explanation: Land rent is a fixed cost because it does not change with the level of production.

quiz.q: Why is a cash flow plan important for a vegetable farm?
options: A) It shows when you need to borrow money
C) It replaces the need for records
quiz.explanation: A cash flow plan helps you anticipate periods of negative cash balance so you can arrange financing.

quiz.q: What is the best way to track daily expenses on a small farm?
options: A) Remember them and write at the end of the month
B) Use a notebook and record immediately
D) Ask your spouse to remember
quiz.explanation: Recording expenses immediately prevents forgetting and ensures accuracy.

quiz.q: Which category would 'transport to market' fall under?
quiz.explanation: Transport is typically grouped under miscellaneous or a separate transport category.

quiz.q: Why should you separate personal and farm money?
options: A) To make tracking farm finances easier
B) To hide money from tax
quiz.explanation: Separating funds allows you to accurately calculate farm profit and loss.

quiz.q: What is the formula for cost of production per kg?
quiz.explanation: Cost of production per kg is total cost divided by total yield in kg.

quiz.q: If total cost is 80,000 KES and yield is 20,000 kg, what is COP per kg?
Why is it important to know your cost of production?
options: A) To set a minimum selling price
quiz.explanation: Knowing COP helps you avoid selling below cost and making a loss.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an indirect cost for a vegetable crop?
quiz.explanation: Depreciation of tools is an indirect cost shared across crops.

quiz.q: What is break-even point?
options: A) The point where total revenue equals total cost
B) The point where profit is maximum
C) The point where yield is highest
D) The point where you start planting
quiz.explanation: Break-even is when revenue covers all costs, resulting in zero profit.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 20,000 KES, selling price is 20 KES/kg, and variable cost is 3 KES/kg, what is break-even quantity?
quiz.explanation: Break-even = fixed costs / (price - variable cost) = 20,000 / 17 = 1,176 kg.

quiz.q: What does contribution margin represent?
options: A) Selling price minus variable cost
B) Total revenue minus total cost
C) Fixed cost plus variable cost
quiz.explanation: Contribution margin is the amount each unit contributes to covering fixed costs.

quiz.q: Why should you calculate break-even before planting?
options: A) To decide if the crop is viable
quiz.explanation: Break-even analysis helps you determine if expected yield and price will cover costs.

quiz.q: In many African countries, small farms are exempt from income tax if:
options: A) Income is below a certain threshold
C) They have less than 1 hectare
quiz.explanation: Tax exemptions often apply to agricultural income below a set limit, such as 1 million KES in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is crop insurance?
options: A) Protection against yield losses due to disasters
B) A loan for buying seeds
quiz.explanation: Crop insurance compensates farmers for losses from drought, floods, pests, etc.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a government-subsidised insurance programme in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: The Agriculture Insurance Subsidy Programme (AISP) subsidises premiums for selected crops.

quiz.q: Why might a small farmer join a farmer group for risk management?
options: A) To pool risk and access emergency loans
quiz.explanation: Farmer groups can provide mutual support and access to credit after disasters.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for farm record keeping?
quiz.explanation: A notebook is a low-cost, effective tool for recording daily transactions.

quiz.q: Which app is mentioned as useful for farm management?
quiz.explanation: Farmbrite is a farm management app that helps track expenses and income.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using farm management software?
options: A) It saves time and reduces errors
C) It eliminates need for labour
quiz.explanation: Software automates calculations and keeps records organised, reducing mistakes.

quiz.q: Which of these is an offline-friendly feature to look for in a farm app?
quiz.explanation: Offline mode is important in rural areas with poor internet connectivity.

quiz.q: What information should you record for every sale?
options: A) Date, crop, quantity, price, buyer
quiz.explanation: Detailed sales records help track profitability and manage customer relations.

quiz.q: Why is it important to update your budget with actual figures?
options: A) To compare planned vs actual and improve
quiz.explanation: Comparing actual to budget helps identify variances and adjust future plans.

quiz.q: What is the break-even revenue if break-even quantity is 1,176 kg and price is 20 KES/kg?
quiz.explanation: Break-even revenue = 1,176 kg * 20 KES/kg = 23,520 KES.

quiz.q: Which cost is likely to be variable for a vegetable farm?
quiz.explanation: Packaging materials vary with the quantity of produce harvested and sold.

quiz.q: What is a key reason to keep farm records for tax purposes?
options: A) To prove income and claim deductions
quiz.explanation: Records substantiate your income and expenses if you are audited or need to claim exemptions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a mobile money service useful for separating farm funds?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa and similar services allow you to keep farm money separate from personal funds.

quiz.q: What is the first step in creating a farm budget?
options: A) List all expected costs and income
quiz.explanation: A budget starts with listing all anticipated expenses and revenue sources.

quiz.q: Why is break-even analysis useful when prices fluctuate?
options: A) It helps decide whether to plant at all
B) It guarantees a fixed price
quiz.explanation: If break-even cannot be met at current prices, you may choose a different crop or delay planting.
